title: Sweet is your will
hook: a line about sweetness that Sikh tradition ties to Guru Arjan's death in Lahore, and to accepting God's will (Guru Granth Sahib 394)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the uncut self, the part Krishna says no weapon cuts and no fire burns. Your line was uncut. Where did you feel something hold steady? Today, a Guru, and a hard kind of sweetness. Day seven hundred twenty-seven.

Tera kiya meetha laagai. Sikhs sing this line, and it means, roughly: what you do tastes sweet to me. On paper it sounds like a line for a good day. A wedding. A new baby. A harvest in. But Sikh memory doesn't file it under good days. It ties the line to Guru Arjan, one of the Sikh Gurus, and to the end of his life. Tradition says he was arrested and held in Lahore, tortured there, and died. And tradition says this was the line he lived inside while it happened. Sweet, said by a man in that place. Today: sweet is your will.
screen: `TERA KIYA MEETHA LAAGAI.` → `A LINE FOR A GOOD DAY?` → `SIKH MEMORY TIES IT TO LAHORE.`

segments.voice: First, the line itself. It sits on page 394 of the Guru Granth Sahib, in a hymn by Guru Arjan, and it runs, in paraphrase: your doing seems sweet to me; Nanak asks for the treasure of the Name. Nanak there is a signature: the later Gurus sign their hymns with the first Guru's name. Notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't say what you do is easy, or fair, or what I'd have chosen. Meetha is a taste word, sweet in the mouth. And the hymn asks for one thing back. Not a way out. The Name. Second, the story. Sikh tradition tells that the Guru was made to sit on a hot iron plate while burning sand was poured over him. The accounts differ in their details, and historians weigh them. What tradition holds onto most is not the cruelty but his calm. Third, the friend. Tradition says the Sufi saint Mian Mir, a Muslim and a friend of the Guru, came and offered to step in and plead for him. And the Guru asked him not to. This too, he said in the story, is the will. Sikhs have a word for that will: bhana, what pleases God. They speak of accepting the bhana, and they remember Guru Arjan as a picture of it. Fourth, what it isn't. Accepting the will, in Sikh teaching, is not folding your hands or calling evil good. The same tradition remembers his death as a wrong done to him, and honors him as a martyr. And it holds acceptance right beside chardi kala, rising spirits, the Sikh phrase this path met in its first year. Acceptance here isn't defeat. It's refusing to let the pain decide who you are.
screen: `A TASTE WORD: MEETHA, SWEET.` · `THE HOT PLATE AND THE CALM.` · `A FRIEND OFFERS TO STEP IN.` · `NOT DEFEAT: RISING SPIRITS.` · then, large: `SWEET IS YOUR WILL.`

segments.voice: Settle into your seat and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one thing you can't change. Not the biggest one. Something you can hold for two minutes: a delay, a diagnosis, a choice someone else already made. Breathe in, and say inside, this is what is. Breathe out, and notice whether any part of you is pushing against it: the jaw, the shoulders, the stomach. Let that one place stop pushing for a breath or two. Nobody is asking you to call it sweet. If you pray, you can hold the Guru's line, tera kiya meetha laagai. If you don't, the plain words this is what is will do. The bell holds the time.
Sweet is your will. From Guru Arjan's line on page 394: your doing tastes sweet. Accepting what can't be changed, without going bitter and without giving up. Today's word.
Your line: sweet is your will. Today, when one thing doesn't go your way, say this is what is once, before you push back. Then decide what to do. Day seven hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing tera kiya meetha laagai in kirtan, and they remember Guru Arjan's martyrdom with gatherings and with chhabeel, stalls that offer cool sweetened water to anyone passing by.

fork.setup: you're Guru Arjan, held in Lahore. your friend Mian Mir, a Sufi saint, offers to step in and plead for you. what do you say?
options: help me find a way to escape.
don't: this too is the will.
fork.reveal: tradition says the Guru asked his friend not to intervene and accepted what came. it's a story Sikhs tell; the details vary between accounts.

original.note: Punjabi in Gurmukhi script: sweet. from the line ਤੇਰਾ ਕੀਆ ਮੀਠਾ ਲਾਗੈ, your doing seems sweet.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line for good days, when life already tastes sweet.
what it means: a line for hard days: God's doing is tasted as sweet, and the hymn asks for the Name, not an escape.
what a scholar hears: page 394 of the Guru Granth Sahib, a hymn of Guru Arjan; Sikh memory ties it to his death in Lahore, though the hymn itself doesn't say when it was written.

notes: Claims rule: the index hook's '1606' and 'the fifth Sikh Guru' are not stated in the cited line, so the script cuts them and says 'one of the Sikh Gurus'; the index line itself still carries them. The arrest, torture and death in Lahore are given as 'tradition says'.

Ang 394 paraphrased: 'Tera kiya meetha laagai, har naam padaarath Nanak maangai' (Asa, Mahala 5). Confirm the Ang, the attribution to Guru Arjan, and the paraphrase 'your doing seems sweet to me; Nanak asks for the treasure of the Name'. Macauliffe's exact wording not quoted.
Hot iron plate and burning sand: the traditional account (Macauliffe vol. 3 tells it); confirm framing, and that 'historians weigh them' is fair.

Mian Mir's offer to intervene and the Guru's refusal: a widely told Sikh story; framed as tradition. Confirm, and confirm the Muslim saint is presented as a friend, with no blame on any community. The authorities who killed him are deliberately not named; a Keeper may prefer naming the Mughal authorities.
Bhana (ਭਾਣਾ) and 'accepting the bhana' as Sikh usage: confirm. 'The picture many hold up' is a soft generalization; cut if a Keeper prefers.
howItsDone: chhabeel on Guru Arjan's martyrdom day; confirm.
Original: ਮੀਠਾ, pronunciation MEE-thah (aspirated retroflex th); confirm spelling and the Gurmukhi of the line.
Editor: fixed a garbled practice line ('this is what is will do' now 'the plain words this is what is will do').

Audit: the teach now explains that 'Nanak' in a hymn by Guru Arjan is the signature the later Gurus use, so listeners don't think Guru Nanak wrote it; the myth reveal names Guru Arjan signing as Nanak.
